# Figure and axes {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Two objects

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`fig`** — the page.

Size, resolution, saving.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**`ax`** — one set of axes on it.

Lines, labels, limits.
:::
:::

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_ylabel("head (m)")
fig.savefig("out.png", dpi=300)
```

::: {.fragment}
Almost everything you want is a method on one or the other. Knowing which is
half of learning matplotlib.
:::

<!-- Figure recovered from old_slides/hwrs564a_oct14.pdf, p. 29. -->
## Most visible elements belong to an `Axes` {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="66%"}
![](../assets/legacy/matplotlib_anatomy.png){fig-alt="Annotated matplotlib figure identifying the figure, axes, lines, markers, labels, ticks, legend, grid, and spines" width="72%"}
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
**The `Figure` owns**

- the canvas
- its size and resolution
- saving the result

**An `Axes` owns**

- the plotted data
- limits, ticks, and labels
- titles, legends, and grids
:::
:::

## `plt.plot` draws somewhere

```python
plt.plot(x, y)        # ...on whatever axes matplotlib touched last
ax.plot(x, y)         # ...here
```

::: {.fragment}
With one plot per cell, they behave identically. With two figures, a loop, or a
function that makes a plot, the `plt.` version starts drawing on the wrong axes
and the bug is invisible in the code.
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
**Always `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` first, then `ax.something()`.** It is one
extra line and it removes an entire category of confusion.
:::

<!-- Figure recovered from old_slides/hwrs564a_oct14.pdf, pp. 30-40. -->
## Panels are an array of `Axes` {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
![](../assets/legacy/multiple_axes_profiles.jpg){fig-alt="Three side-by-side soil pressure-head profiles comparing simulated and analytical solutions" width="96%"}
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}
```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3,
                         sharey=True)

axes[0].plot(...)
axes[1].plot(...)
axes[2].plot(...)
```

One figure owns three axes. Each `axes[i]` receives its own data and labels.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
With a 2 × 2 layout, `axes` is a 2 × 2 array; `axes.flat` iterates it in reading
order. The indexing idea does not change.
:::

## Sharing an axis is a claim

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, sharey=True)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **`sharey=True`** puts every panel on the same scale, so the panels are
  comparable
- **`sharey=False`** lets each panel fill its own range
:::

::: {.fragment}
Three wells with 6 ft, 110 ft, and 30 ft of decline look **identical** on
independent axes. Sharing the axis is what makes the comparison honest.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And don't share when the quantities aren't comparable — that makes one panel
look flat for no reason.
:::

## Your turn: two stacked panels

Discharge on top, its 7-day mean below, sharing the x axis so they line up.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_panels
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np, pandas as pd
idx = pd.date_range("2006-01-01", periods=365, freq="D")
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(365) / 58)) * 40 + rng.gamma(1, 3, 365), index=idx)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_panels
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4), sharex=______)
axes[0].plot(q.index, q, color="#AB0520", lw=0.8)
axes[0].set_ylabel(______)
axes[1].plot(q.index, q.rolling(7, center=True).mean(), color="#0C234B", lw=1.6)
axes[1].set_ylabel("7-day mean (cfs)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_panels"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Sharing takes a boolean. The label needs the quantity *and* its unit.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_panels"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 4), sharex=True)
axes[0].set_ylabel("daily discharge (cfs)")
```

With `sharex=True` the top panel's tick labels disappear automatically, which is
what you want — one set of dates for both panels, and more room for the data.
:::
:::

# Colour {background-color="#AB0520"}

## Three kinds, three jobs

| Data | Colormap |
|---|---|
| runs one way, low to high | **sequential** — `viridis`, `Blues` |
| has a meaningful middle | **diverging** — `RdBu`, `coolwarm` |
| unordered categories | **qualitative** — `tab10` |

::: {.fragment}
Using a diverging map on sequential data puts a false boundary in the middle of
your range. Using a sequential map on diverging data hides the zero crossing.
:::

<!-- Figure recovered from old_slides/hwrs564a_oct14.pdf, p. 23. -->
## `jet` changes apparent structure {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="66%"}
![](../assets/legacy/colormap_perception.png){fig-alt="The same Earth, apple, and portrait shown in grayscale, the jet rainbow colormap, and the perceptually uniform batlow colormap" width="98%"}
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
**`jet`** adds bright cyan and yellow bands and dark ends.

**Perceptual maps** vary more steadily, so equal data steps look more nearly equal.

Use `viridis`, `cividis`, or another perceptually uniform map for ordered data.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
`jet` can invent boundaries that are not in the data and hide ones that are.
:::

## Centre a diverging map on zero

```python
limit = change["ft"].abs().max()
ax.scatter(..., cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-limit, vmax=limit)
```

::: {.fragment}
Leave `vmin`/`vmax` off and matplotlib centres on the **midpoint of your data**.
With changes from −6 to +111 ft, the neutral colour lands at +52 — so wells that
dropped fifty feet render as "unchanged".
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
A diverging colormap that isn't centred on zero says the opposite of what you
mean, in a way that looks completely normal.
:::

## Your turn: centre the colormap

These changes run from −6 to +111 ft. Make zero the neutral colour.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_diverge
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(88)
lon = -111.2 + rng.random(60) * 0.45
lat = 32.0 + rng.random(60) * 0.45
change = np.concatenate([rng.uniform(-6, 0, 7), rng.uniform(0, 111, 53)])
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_diverge
limit = ______

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.5))
sc = ax.scatter(lon, lat, c=change, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=______, vmax=______, s=40)
fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, label="change in depth to water (ft)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_diverge"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

You want the limits symmetric about zero, so both come from the *largest
absolute* value in the data.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_diverge"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
limit = np.abs(change).max()
sc = ax.scatter(..., vmin=-limit, vmax=limit, ...)
```

Now white means zero and the seven recovering wells are visibly on the other
side of it. Without the limits, matplotlib centres on the data midpoint of about
+52 ft — so a well that dropped fifty feet renders white and reads as unchanged.

The cost is that most of the blue half of the colorbar goes unused. That is
fine: an unused range is honest, a mislabelled midpoint is not.
:::
:::

## Colour cannot be the only signal

::: {.incremental}
- About one reader in twelve has a colour vision deficiency
- Deuteranopia makes red and green nearly identical
- Projectors and photocopiers do their own damage
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Encode every distinction at least twice.**

```python
ax.plot(x, a, color="#AB0520", ls="-",  marker="o", label="pumped")
ax.plot(x, b, color="#0C234B", ls="--", marker="s", label="control")
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two extra keyword arguments. The figure now works in greyscale, on a bad
projector, and for everyone in the room.
:::

## Your turn: make it readable

This uses red and green, and nothing else, to tell two series apart.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_color
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, numpy as np
years = np.arange(2005, 2025)
rng = np.random.default_rng(564)
a = 40 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(1.2, 2.0, 20))
b = 40 + np.cumsum(rng.normal(0.3, 2.0, 20))
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_color
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
ax.plot(years, a, color="#AB0520", ls="-",  ______, label="heavily pumped")
ax.plot(years, b, color="#0C234B", ls=______, marker="s", label="lightly pumped")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.set_ylabel("depth to water (ft)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_color"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The first line needs a marker; the second needs a dash pattern that differs from
the first. `"--"`, `"-."`, and `":"` are all available.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_color"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
ax.plot(years, a, color="#AB0520", ls="-",  marker="o", label="heavily pumped")
ax.plot(years, b, color="#0C234B", ls="--", marker="s", label="lightly pumped")
```

Note the colours also changed — UA red and blue differ in *lightness*, not just
hue, so they survive a greyscale print. Red and green are nearly the same
lightness, which is why that pair fails twice over.
:::
:::
